nodes.name: Proof of Derivatives of H2, H3, H4
nodes.statement: Equivalences are obvious from the definition of the Serre derivative. Define $f_{2}, f_{3}, f_{4}$ be the differences of the left and right hand sides of \eqref{eqn:H2-serre-der}, \eqref{eqn:H3-serre-der}, \eqref{eqn:H4-serre-der}. \begin{align} f_{2} &:= \partial_{2} H_{2} - \frac{1}{6} H_{2}(H_{2} + 2H_{4}) \\ f_{3} &:= \partial_{2} H_{3} - \frac{1}{6} (H_{2}^2 - H_{4}^2) \\ f_{4} &:= \partial_{2} H_{4} + \frac{1}{6} H_{4}(2H_{2} + H_{4}). \end{align} Then these are a priori modular forms of weight $4$ and level $\Gamma(2)$, and our goal is to prove that they are actually zeros. By Jacobi's identity \eqref{eqn:jacobi-identity}, we have $f_{2} + f_{4} = f_{3}$. Also, the transformation rules of $H_2, H_3, H_4$ give \begin{align} f_{2}|_{S} &= -f_{4} \\ f_{2}|_{T} &= -f_{2} \\ f_{4}|_{S} &= -f_{2} \\ f_{4}|_{T} &= f_{3} = f_{2} + f_{4}. \end{align} Now, define \begin{align} g &:= (2 H_2 + H_4) f_2 + (H_2 + 2 H_4) f_4 \\ h &:= f_{2}^{2} + f_{2}f_{4} + f_{4}^{2}. \end{align} Then one can check that both $g$ and $h$ are invariant under the actions of $S$ and $T$, hence they are modular forms of level $1$. Also, by analyzing the limit of $g$ and $h$ as $z \to i \infty$, one can see that $g$ and $h$ are cusp forms, hence $g = h = 0$ by \eqref{eqn:dimS6} and \eqref{eqn:dimS8}. This implies \begin{align} 3 E_4 f_2^{2} &= 3 (H_2^2 + H_2 H_4 + H_4^2) f_2^{2} = ((2 H_2 + H_4)^{2} - (2H_2 + H_4)(H_2 + 2H_4) + (H_2 + 2H_4)^{2}) f_2^{2}\\ &= (2 H_2 + H_4)^{2} (f_2^2 + f_2 f_4 + f_4^2) = 0 \end{align} and by considering $q$-series ($E_4$ has an invertible $q$-series), we get $f_2 = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the defect forms $f_2,f_3,f_4$ and show they vanish using level one cusp forms $g,h$. Key step: $3E_4f_2^2=(2H_2+H_4)^2h=0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Polynomial bound for the auxiliary integral
nodes.statement: Fix $n \in \N$. We know there exists a constant $C$ such that for all $x \geq 0$, $\abs{x}^n \cdot \abs{e^{-\pi x}} \leq C$. In particular, for all $r \geq 0$ and $s \geq 1$, $r^n \cdot e^{-\pi r/s} \leq C s^n$. Hence, for all $r \in \R$, we can write \begin{align} r^n \cdot \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, e^{-\pi r /s} \, \dd{s} = \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, \left(\abs{r}^n \cdot e^{-\pi r /s}\right) \, \dd{s} \leq C \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} \end{align} The $\Gamma$ function is given by \begin{align} \Gamma(x) = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u} \, u^{x-1} \, \dd{u} \end{align} for all $x > 0$. Hence, writing $u = 2\pi s$ and using $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$, we get \begin{align} C \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} \leq C \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} = C \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n+1}} e^{-u} \, u^n \, \dd{u} = \frac{C}{(2\pi)^n} \Gamma(n+1) = \frac{C \cdot n!}{(2\pi)^n} \end{align} Defining $C' := \frac{C \cdot n!}{(2\pi)^n}$ finishes the proof.

nodes.statement: Suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lemma:theta-transform-S-T}, we have \begin{align} H_2|_{-2}ST = (-H_4)|_{-2}T = -H_3, \\ H_3|_{-2}ST = (-H_3)|_{-2}T = -H_4, \\ H_4|_{-2}ST = (-H_2)|_{-2}T = H_2. \end{align} Using these equations and Lemma \ref{lemma:lv1-lv2-identities}, we can rewrite $\psi_I(z)$ as \begin{align} \psi_I(z) &= h(z) - h|_{-2}ST(z) \\ &= 128 \frac{H_3 + H_4}{H_2^2} - 128 \frac{-H_4 + H_2}{H_3^2} \\ &= 128 \frac{H_3^2 (H_3 + H_4) - H_2^2 (H_2 - H_4)}{H_2^2 H_3^2} \\ &= 128 \frac{(H_2 + H_4)^2 (H_2 + 2 H_4) - H_2^2 (H_2 - H_4)}{H_2^2 H_3^2} \\ &= 128 \frac{H_4(5 H_2^2 + 5 H_2 H_4 + 2 H_4^2)}{ H_2^2 H_3^2} \\ &= 128 \frac{H_4^3(5 H_2^2 + 5 H_2 H_4 + 2 H_4^2)}{ H_2^2 H_3^2 H_4^3} \\ &= \frac{H_4^3 (5 H_2^2 + 5 H_2 H_4 + 2 H_4^2)}{2\Delta}. \end{align} Applying $|_{-2}S$ and $|_{-2}T$ to the expression of $\psi_I$ proves \eqref{eqn:psiS-new} and \eqref{eqn:psiT-new}.

nodes.name: Proof of b is a Fourier eigenfunction with eigenvalue -1
nodes.statement:
Here, we repeat the arguments used in the proof of Proposition~ef{prop:a-fourier}. We use identity~\eqref{eqn:gaussian Fourier} and change contour integration in $z$ and Fourier transform in $x$. Thus we obtain  egin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 ( rac{-1}{z})}\,dz + \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 ( rac{-1}{z})}\,dz 
otag \ -& 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 ( rac{-1}{z})}\,dz - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 ( rac{-1}{z})}\,dz. 
otag \end{align} We make the change of variables $w= rac{-1}{z}$ and arrive at  egin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T\Big( rac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T\Big( rac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw 
otag \ -& 2\,\int\limits_{i\infty}^{i}\psi_I\Big( rac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{0}\psi_S\Big( rac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.
otag \end{align} Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn:psiI-define}--\eqref{eqn:psiS-define} imply  egin{align} \psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T 
otag \ \psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S 
otag \ \psi_S|_{-2}S=&\psi_I. 
otag \end{align} Therefore, we arrive at  egin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz 
otag \ +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.
otag \end{align} Now from~\eqref{eqn:b-definition} we see that $$ \mathcal{F}(b)(x)=-b(x). $$

nodes.statement:
We denote the right hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} by $c(r)$. By Corollary ef{cor:psiI-near-0-infty}, the integral in~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} converges for $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then we rewrite it in the following way: $$c(r)=\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz-2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.$$ From the Fourier expansion~\eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we know that $\psi_I(z)=e^{-2\pi i z}+O(1)$ as $\Im(z)	o\infty$. By assumption $r^2>2$, hence we can deform the path of integration and write  egin{align} \int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align} We have  egin{align}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\ &+2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}(\psi_T(z)-\psi_I(z))\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.
onumber \end{align} Next, we check that the functions $\psi_I,\psi_T$, and $\psi_S$ satisfy the following identity:  egin{equation}\psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I.\end{equation} Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn:psiI-define}-\eqref{eqn:psiS-define} we get  egin{align}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S
otag\ =&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.
otag\end{align} Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$ Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore, $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h|_{-2}-h|ST=\psi_I.$$ Combining \eqref{eqn: c1} and \eqref{eqn: c2} we find  egin{align}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz
otag\ &-2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz
otag\ =&b(r).
otag \end{align}

nodes.name: Proof of Integral representation of b
nodes.statement: The proof is analogous to the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:a-another-integral}. First, suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop:b-double-zeros} $$b(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\psi_I(it)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$ From \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we obtain \begin{equation} \psi_I(it)=e^{2\pi t}+144+O(e^{-\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{equation} For $r>\sqrt{2}$ we have \begin{equation} \int\limits_0^\infty \left(e^{2\pi t}+144\right)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt =\frac{1}{\pi\,(r^2-2)}+\frac{144}{\pi\,r^2}.\end{equation} Therefore, the identity \eqref{eqn:b-another-integral} holds for $r>\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, from the definition \eqref{eqn:b-definition} we see that $b(r)$ is analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. The asymptotic expansion \eqref{eqn: psi asymptotic} implies that the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:b-another-integral} is also analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$. Hence, the identity \eqref{eqn:b-another-integral} holds on the whole interval $[0,\infty)$. This finishes the proof of the proposition.

nodes.statement: F(it) - \frac{18}{\pi^2} G(it) < 0
nodes.label: eqn:ineqBnew

nodes.name: Proof of Reformulation of the inequalities in terms of F and G
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eqn:psiS-define}, \begin{equation} \psi_I(it) = (\psi_S|_{-2}S)(it) = (it)^{2}\psi_S\left(-\frac{1}{it}\right) = -t^2 \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right). \end{equation} Combined with Lemma \ref{lemma:F-G-phi-psi-identities} we can rewrite \eqref{eqn:ineqA} as \begin{equation} A(t) = -t^2 \phi_0\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) + \frac{36}{\pi^2} \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) < 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{F(it)}{\Delta(it)} + \frac{18}{\pi^2} \frac{G(it)}{\Delta(it)} > 0 \end{equation} for $t > 0$, which is equivalent to \eqref{eqn:ineqAnew} by Corollary \ref{cor:disc-pos}. Equivalences of \eqref{eqn:ineqB} and \eqref{eqn:ineqBnew} follows similarly; just change the sign.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $\psi_I(it)$ via $\psi_S(i/t)$, express in $F,G$, divide by $\Delta(it)>0$.

nodes.name: Equation (212)
nodes.statement: \psi_I(it) = (\psi_S|_{-2}S)(it) = (it)^{2}\psi_S\left(-\frac{1}{it}\right) = -t^2 \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right).

nodes.name: Equation (213)
nodes.statement: A(t) = -t^2 \phi_0\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) + \frac{36}{\pi^2} \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) < 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{F(it)}{\Delta(it)} + \frac{18}{\pi^2} \frac{G(it)}{\Delta(it)} > 0

nodes.name: Positivity of F and G on the imaginary axis
nodes.statement: For all $t > 0$, we have $F(it) > 0$ and $G(it) > 0$.
nodes.label: lemma:F-G-pos

nodes.name: Proof of Positivity of F and G on the imaginary axis
nodes.statement: By Ramanujan's identity \eqref{eqn:DE4}, we have $F(z) = 9 E_4'(z)^2$ and \begin{equation} F(it) = 9E_4'(it)^2 = 9 \left(240\sum_{n \geq 1} n \sigma_3(n) e^{-2 \pi n t} \right)^{2} > 0. \end{equation} $G(it) > 0$ follows from positivity of $H_2(it)$ and $H_4(it)$ (Lemma \ref{cor:theta-pos}).
nodes.statement_short: $F=9E_4'^2$ has positive series; $G>0$ from theta positivity.

nodes.name: Equation (214)
nodes.statement: F(it) = 9E_4'(it)^2 = 9 \left(240\sum_{n \geq 1} n \sigma_3(n) e^{-2 \pi n t} \right)^{2} > 0.

nodes.name: First inequality for F and G
nodes.statement: \eqref{eqn:ineqAnew} holds.
nodes.label: cor:ineqAnew

nodes.name: Proof of First inequality for F and G
nodes.statement: This directly follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:F-G-pos}.

nodes.name: Modular linear differential equations for F and G
nodes.statement: $F$ and $G$ satisfy the following differential equations: \begin{align} \partial_{12}\partial_{10} F - \frac{5}{6} E_{4} F &= 7200 \Delta (-E_{2}') \\ \partial_{12}\partial_{10} G - \frac{5}{6} E_{4} G &= -640 \Delta H_{2} \end{align}
nodes.label: lemma:FG-de

nodes.name: Equation (215)
nodes.statement: \partial_{12}\partial_{10} F - \frac{5}{6} E_{4} F &= 7200 \Delta (-E_{2}')
nodes.label: eqn:ddf

nodes.name: Equation (216)
nodes.statement: \partial_{12}\partial_{10} G - \frac{5}{6} E_{4} G &= -640 \Delta H_{2}
nodes.label: eqn:ddg

nodes.name: Proof of Modular linear differential equations for F and G
nodes.statement: Both can be shown by direct computations. By Ramanujan's identities (Theorem \ref{thm:ramanujan-formula}) and the product rule of Serre derivatives (Theorem \ref{thm:serre-der-prod-rule}), we have \begin{align} \partial_{5} (E_2 E_4 - E_6) &= (E_2 E_4 - E_6)' - \frac{5}{12} E_2 (E_2 E_4 - E_6) \\ &= \frac{E_2^2 - E_4}{12} \cdot E_4 + E_2 \cdot \frac{E_2 E_4 - E_6}{3} - \frac{E_2 E_6 - E_4^2}{2} - \frac{5}{12}E_2 (E_2 E_4 - E_6) \\ &= -\frac{5}{12} (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2) \\ \partial_{7} (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2) &= (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)' - \frac{7}{12} E_2 (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2) \\ &= \frac{E_2^2 - E_4}{12} \cdot E_6 + E_2 \cdot \frac{E_2 E_6 - E_4^2}{2} - 2 E_4 \cdot \frac{E_2 E_4 - E_6}{3} - \frac{7}{12} E_2 (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2) \\ &= -\frac{7}{12} E_4 (E_2 E_4 - E_6) \end{align} and using these we can compute \begin{align} \partial_{10} F &= \partial_{10} (E_2 E_4 - E_6)^2 \\ &= 2 (E_2 E_4 - E_6) \partial_{5} (E_2 E_4 - E_6) \\ &= -\frac{5}{6} (E_2 E_4 - E_6) (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2), \\ \partial_{12}\partial_{10} F &= -\frac{5}{6} \partial_{12} ((E_2 E_4 - E_6) (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)) \\ &= -\frac{5}{6} (\partial_{5}(E_2 E_4 - E_6)) (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2) - \frac{5}{6} (E_2 E_4 - E_6) (\partial_{7} (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)) \\ &= \frac{25}{72} (E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)^2 + \frac{35}{72} E_4 (E_2 E_4 - E_6)^2, \\ \partial_{12}\partial_{10}F - \frac{5}{6} E_4 F &= \frac{25}{72}(E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)^2 + \frac{35}{72} E_4 (E_2 E_4 - E_6)^2 - \frac{5}{6} E_4 (E_2 E_4 - E_6)^2 \\ &= \frac{25}{72} ((E_2 E_6 - E_4^2)^2 - E_4 (E_2 E_4 - E_6)^2) \\ &= \frac{25}{72} (- E_2^2 E_4^3 + E_2^2 E_6^2 + E_4^4 - E_4 E_6^3) \\ &= -\frac{25}{72} (E_4^3 - E_6^2) (E_2^2 - E_4) \\ &= 7200 \cdot \frac{E_4^3 - E_6^2}{1728} \cdot \frac{-E_2^2 + E_4}{12}\\ &= 7200 \Delta (-E_2') \end{align} which proves \eqref{eqn:ddf}. Similarly, \eqref{eqn:ddg} can be proved using Proposition \ref{prop:theta-der} and Lemma \ref{lemma:lv1-lv2-identities}.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation with Ramanujan's identities and the Serre product rule.

nodes.name: Signs of the MLDE right-hand sides
nodes.statement: \eqref{eqn:ddf} (resp. \eqref{eqn:ddg}) is positive (resp. negative) on the (positive) imaginary axis.
nodes.label: cor:MLDE-pos

nodes.name: Proof of Signs of the MLDE right-hand sides
nodes.statement: From \eqref{eqn:E2} and Lemma \ref{cor:disc-pos}, \ifplastex \begin{equation*} 7200 (-E_2'(it)) \Delta(it) = 7200 \cdot 24 \left(\sum_{n \ge 1} n \sigma_1(n) e^{-2 \pi n t}\right) \cdot \Delta(it) > 0. \end{equation*} \else \begin{equation} 7200 (-E_2'(it)) \Delta(it) = 7200 \cdot 24 \left(\sum_{n \ge 1} n \sigma_1(n) e^{-2 \pi n t}\right) \cdot \Delta(it) > 0. \notag \end{equation} \fi Negativity of \eqref{eqn:ddg}, i.e. $-640 \Delta(it) H_2(it) < 0$ follows from Corollary \ref{cor:theta-pos} and \ref{cor:disc-pos}.
nodes.statement_short: Positivity of $-E_2'$ series and of $\Delta$, $H_2$ on the imaginary axis.

nodes.name: Quotient Q
nodes.statement: Since $G(it) > 0$ for all $t > 0$, we can define the quotient \begin{equation} Q(t) := \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} \end{equation} as a function on $(0, \infty)$.

nodes.name: Equation (235)
nodes.statement: Q(t) := \frac{F(it)}{G(it)}
nodes.label: eqn:Q

nodes.name: Limit of Q at 0
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0^+} Q(t) = \frac{18}{\pi^2}. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lemma:Qlim

nodes.name: Proof of Limit of Q at 0
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0^+} Q(t) = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F(i/t)}{G(i/t)}. \end{equation} By using the transformation laws of Eisenstein series \eqref{eqn:E2-S-transform}, \eqref{eqn:Ek-trans-S} (for $k = 4, 6$) and the thetanull functions, \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-S}, \eqref{eqn:H4-transform-S}, we get \begin{align} F\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) &= t^{12} F(it) - \frac{12t^{11}}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36t^{10}}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2, \\ G\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) &= t^{10} H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2}). \end{align} Since $F$, $E_2 E_4 - E_6$ and $H_2$ are cusp forms, we have $\lim_{t \to \infty}t^k A(it) = 0$ when $A(z)$ is one of these forms and $k \geq 0$. From $\lim_{t \to \infty} E_4(it) = 1 = \lim_{t \to \infty}H_{4}(it)$, we get \begin{align} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F(i/t)}{G(i/t)} &= \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{t^{12} F(it) - \frac{12t^{11}}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36t^{10}}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2}{t^{10} H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2})} \\ &= \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{t^{2} F(it) - \frac{12t}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2}{H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2})} \\ &= \frac{18}{\pi^2}. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Substitute $t\to1/t$, apply transformation laws and take limits using cusp form decay.

nodes.name: Equation (237)
nodes.statement: \lim_{t \to 0^+} Q(t) = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F(i/t)}{G(i/t)}.

nodes.name: Logarithmic derivative at infinity
nodes.statement: Let $F$ be a quasimodular form where the vanishing order of $F$ at infinity is $n_0 > 0$, i.e. $F(z) = \sum_{n \geq n_0} a_n q^{n}$ with $a_{n_0} \ne 0$. Then \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} = n_0. \end{equation}
assumptions: Let $F$ be a quasimodular form where the vanishing order of $F$ at infinity is $n_0 > 0$, i.e. $F(z) = \sum_{n \geq n_0} a_n q^{n}$ with $a_{n_0} \ne 0$.
conclusions: Let $F$ be a quasimodular form where the vanishing order of $F$ at infinity is $n_0 > 0$, i.e. $F(z) = \sum_{n \geq n_0} a_n q^{n}$ with $a_{n_0} \ne 0$. Then \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} = n_0. \end{equation}
nodes.label: lemma:log-der-inf

nodes.name: Equation (243)
nodes.statement: \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} = n_0.

nodes.name: Proof of Logarithmic derivative at infinity
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{lemma:der-q-series}, \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} n a_n e^{-2 \pi n t}}{\sum_{n \ge n_0} a_n e^{-2 \pi n t}} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{n_0 a_{n_0} e^{-2 \pi n_0 t} + O(e^{-2 \pi (n_0 + 1) t})}{a_{n_0} e^{-2 \pi n_0 t} + O(e^{-2 \pi (n_0 + 1) t})} = n_0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Compare leading terms of the $q$-series of $F'$ and $F$.

nodes.name: Equation (244)
nodes.statement: \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} n a_n e^{-2 \pi n t}}{\sum_{n \ge n_0} a_n e^{-2 \pi n t}} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{n_0 a_{n_0} e^{-2 \pi n_0 t} + O(e^{-2 \pi (n_0 + 1) t})}{a_{n_0} e^{-2 \pi n_0 t} + O(e^{-2 \pi (n_0 + 1) t})} = n_0.

nodes.name: Q is strictly decreasing
nodes.statement: The function $t \mapsto Q(t)$ is strictly decreasing.
conclusions: The function $t \mapsto Q(t)$ is strictly decreasing.
nodes.label: prop:Qdec

nodes.name: Proof of Q is strictly decreasing
nodes.statement: It is enough to show that \begin{align} \frac{\dd}{\dd t} \left(\frac{F(it)}{G(it)}\right) < 0 &\Leftrightarrow (- 2\pi) \frac{F'(it)G(it) - F(it) G'(it)}{G(it)^{2}} < 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow F'(it) G(it) - F(it) G'(it) > 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow (\partial_{10}F)(it) G(it) - F(it) (\partial_{10}G)(it) > 0. \end{align} Let $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0} := (\partial_{10}F) G - F (\partial_{10} G) = F'G - FG'$. Then \begin{align} \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}}{FG} = \frac{F'G - FG'}{FG} = \frac{F'}{F} - \frac{G'}{G} \end{align} The vanishing order of $F$ and $G$ at the infinity are $2$ and $\frac{3}{2}$ respectively, so by Lemma \ref{lemma:log-der-inf}, we have \begin{align} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it)}{F(it) G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left(\frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} - \frac{G'(it)}{G(it)}\right) = 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0 \end{align} so $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it) > 0$ for sufficiently large $t$. Its Serre derivative $\partial_{22} \mathcal{L}_{1, 0}$ is positive by Corollary \ref{cor:MLDE-pos}: \begin{align} \partial_{22} \mathcal{L}_{1, 0} = (\partial_{12} \partial_{10} F) G - F (\partial_{12}\partial_{10} G) = \Delta (7200 (-E_{2}') G + 640 H_2 F) > 0. \end{align} Hence $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it) > 0$ by Theorem \ref{thm:anti-serre-der-pos}, and the monotonicity follows.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to positivity of the Wronskian-like $\mathcal{L}_{1,0}$, positive at infinity with positive Serre derivative. Key step: apply the anti-Serre-derivative positivity theorem.

nodes.name: Equation (245)
nodes.statement: \frac{\dd}{\dd t} \left(\frac{F(it)}{G(it)}\right) < 0 &\Leftrightarrow (- 2\pi) \frac{F'(it)G(it) - F(it) G'(it)}{G(it)^{2}} < 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow F'(it) G(it) - F(it) G'(it) > 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow (\partial_{10}F)(it) G(it) - F(it) (\partial_{10}G)(it) > 0.

nodes.name: Equation (248)
nodes.statement: \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}}{FG} = \frac{F'G - FG'}{FG} = \frac{F'}{F} - \frac{G'}{G}

nodes.name: Equation (249)
nodes.statement: \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it)}{F(it) G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left(\frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} - \frac{G'(it)}{G(it)}\right) = 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0

nodes.name: Equation (250)
nodes.statement: \partial_{22} \mathcal{L}_{1, 0} = (\partial_{12} \partial_{10} F) G - F (\partial_{12}\partial_{10} G) = \Delta (7200 (-E_{2}') G + 640 H_2 F) > 0.

nodes.name: Second inequality for F and G
nodes.statement: \eqref{eqn:ineqBnew} holds.
nodes.label: cor:ineqBnew

nodes.name: Proof of Second inequality for F and G
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} = Q(t) < \lim_{u \to 0^+} Q(u) = \frac{18}{\pi^2} \end{equation} and by Lemma \ref{lemma:F-G-pos}, \eqref{eqn:ineqBnew} follows.
nodes.statement_short: $Q(t)$ is below its limit at $0^+$ by monotonicity.

nodes.name: Equation (251)
nodes.statement: \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} = Q(t) < \lim_{u \to 0^+} Q(u) = \frac{18}{\pi^2}

nodes.name: Magic function g
nodes.statement: The function $$g(x):=\frac{\pi\,i}{8640}a(x)+\frac{i}{240\pi}\,b(x)$$ satisfies conditions \eqref{eqn:g1}--\eqref{eqn:g3}.
nodes.statement_short: $g=\frac{\pi i}{8640}a+\frac{i}{240\pi}b$ satisfies the three Cohn-Elkies conditions.
nodes.label: thm:g1

nodes.name: Proof of Magic function g
nodes.statement: First, we prove that \eqref{eqn:g1} holds. By Propositions~\ref{prop:a-double-zeros} and \ref{prop:b-double-zeros} we know that for $r>\sqrt{2}$ \begin{equation} g(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty A(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$A(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ from the Proposition~\ref{prop:ineqA} we know that $A(t)<0\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,\infty).$ Therefore identity \eqref{eqn:g A} implies \eqref{eqn:g1}. Next, we prove \eqref{eqn:g2}. By Propositions~\ref{prop:a-another-integral} and~\ref{prop:b-another-integral} we know that for $r>0$ \begin{equation} \widehat{g}(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty B(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$B(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ Finally, the property \eqref{eqn:g3} readily follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:a0} and Proposition~\ref{prop:b0}. This finishes the proof of Theorems~\ref{thm:g1} and~\ref{thm:g}.
nodes.statement_short: Write $g$ and $\widehat g$ as Laplace-type integrals of $A$ and $B$ and use their signs; values at 0 from $a(0),b(0)$.

nodes.name: Equation (252)
nodes.statement: g(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty A(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt
nodes.label: eqn:g A

nodes.name: Equation (253)
nodes.statement: \widehat{g}(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty B(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt
nodes.label: eqn:g B

nodes.name: Change variables in the limsup
nodes.statement: One can show, using relatively unsophisticated real analysis, that \[ \limsup_{R \to \infty} \Delta_{\Pa(cX)}(R) = \limsup_{cR \to \infty} \Delta_{\Pa(cX)}(cR) \]

nodes.name: Apply finite-density scaling
nodes.statement: Lemma~\ref{SpherePacking.scale_finiteDensity} tells us that $\Delta_{\Pa(cX)}(cR) = \Delta_{\Pa(X)}(R)$ for every $R > 0$.

nodes.name: Conclude by another change of variables
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ \limsup_{cR \to \infty} \Delta_{\Pa(cX)}(cR) = \limsup_{cR \to \infty} \Delta_{\Pa(X)}(R) = \limsup_{R \to \infty} \Delta_{\Pa(X)}(R) \] where the second equality is the result of a similar change of variables to the one done above.
nodes.statement_short: Conclude by another change of variables

nodes.name: Easy direction, set up the reverse inequality
nodes.statement: That the supremum over packings of unit density is at most the sphere packing constant is obvious. For the reverse inequality, let $\Pa(X)$ be any sphere packing with separation radius $r$.
nodes.statement_short: Easy direction, set up the reverse inequality

nodes.name: Density is invariant under rescaling
nodes.statement: We know, from Lemma~\ref{SpherePacking.scale_density}, that the density of $\Pa(X)$ is equal to that of the scaled packing $\Pa\!\left(\frac{X}{r}\right)$.

nodes.name: Bound by the unit-separation supremum
nodes.statement: Since the scaled packing has separation radius $1$, its density is naturally at most the supremum over all packings of unit density, meaning that the same is true of $\Pa(X)$.

nodes.name: Attribution
nodes.statement: The following proof was written by Junyan Xu in the thread for \href{https://github.com/thefundamentaltheor3m/Sphere-Packing-Lean/issues/80}{Issue \#80} of the repository.

nodes.name: State the goal and define density in a set
nodes.statement: Given an arbitrary packing $P$ of upper density $\Delta$ and an arbitrary $\epsilon > 0$, we want to produce a periodic packing with density at least $\Delta - \epsilon$. Given a set $S$ (of nonzero volume), we shall call the quantity $\frac{\left| S \cap P \right|}{\left| S \right|}$ the density of $P$ in $S$, where $\left| S \right|$ denotes the volume of $S$.
nodes.statement_short: State the goal and define density in a set

nodes.name: Choose side length $\ell$ and radius $R_0$
nodes.statement: Choose $\ell > 0$ such that \[ \frac{(\ell - 4r)^d}{\ell^d} > 1 - \frac{\epsilon}{3} \] (where $r$ is the radius of the balls in $P$ and $d$ is the dimension). Then choose $R_0 > 0$ such that for all $R > R_0$, we have \[ \frac{\left( R + \sqrt{d}\,\ell \right)^d - \left( R - \sqrt{d}\,\ell \right)^d}{R^d} < \frac{\epsilon}{3} \]

nodes.name: Pick a large ball with density near $\Delta$
nodes.statement: By definition of upper density, there exists $R > R_0$ such that the density of $P$ in $B(0,R)$ is at least $\Delta - \frac{\epsilon}{3}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick a large ball with density near $\Delta$

nodes.name: Tile by hypercubes; define unions $S\subseteq T$
nodes.statement: The Euclidean space is covered by disjoint hypercubes of side length $\ell$ of the form $\prod_{i=1}^d \left[ n_i\ell, (n_i+1)\ell \right)$ with $n_i \in \mathbb{Z}$. Since these hypercubes have diameter $\sqrt{d}\ell$, those that intersect $B(0,R)$ must be contained in $B(0,R+\sqrt{d}\ell)$. Thus the hypercubes contained in $B(0,R+\sqrt{d}\ell)$ cover $B(0,R)$. Similarly, the hypercubes not contained in $B(0,R)$ cannot intersect $B(0,R-\sqrt{d}\ell)$. Denote the union of hypercubes contained in $B(0,R+\sqrt{d}\ell)$ by $T$ and the union of those contained in $B(0,R)$ by $S$, we then have \[ S \subseteq B(0,R) \subseteq T \subseteq B(0,R+\sqrt{d}\ell) \] and \[ T \setminus S \subseteq B(0,R+\sqrt{d}\ell) \setminus B(0,R-\sqrt{d}\ell) \]
nodes.statement_short: Tile by hypercubes; define unions $S\subseteq T$

nodes.name: Density in $S$ exceeds $\Delta-2\epsilon/3$
nodes.statement: The density of $P$ in $S$ is \[ \begin{aligned} \frac{\left| S \cap P \right|}{\left| S \right|} &\ge \frac{\left| B(0,R) \cap P \right| - \left| B(0,R) \setminus S \right|}{\left| B(0,R) \right|} \\ &> \left( \Delta - \frac{\epsilon}{3} \right) - \frac{\left| T \setminus S \right|}{\left| B(0,R) \right|} \\ &> \left( \Delta - \frac{\epsilon}{3} \right) - \frac{\epsilon}{3} \end{aligned} \]

nodes.name: Periodize a dense hypercube
nodes.statement: Therefore, the density of $P$ in some hypercube $C \subseteq S$ is at least $\Delta - \frac{2\epsilon}{3}$. If a ball in $P$ (thus of diameter $2r$) is not completely contained in $C$, it cannot intersect the hypercube $C'$ with the same center as $C$ with side length $\ell-4r$, so excluding these balls from $C\cap P$ decreases the density in $C$ by at most $\frac{\left| C \setminus C' \right|}{\left| C \right|} = \frac{\ell^d - (\ell-4r)^d}{\ell^d} < \frac{\epsilon}{3}$, and gives rise to a periodic packing of density $> \Delta - \epsilon$ with $C$ as a fundamental domain.

nodes.name: Lower bound: ball covered by fundamental-domain translates
nodes.statement: For the first inequality, it suffices to prove that $\mathcal{B}_d(R - L) \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R)} (x + \mathcal{D})$, since the cosets on the right are disjoint. For a vector $v \in \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)$, we have $\|v\| < R - L$ by definition. Since $\mathcal{D}$ is a fundamental domain, there exists a lattice point $x \in \Lambda$ such that $v \in x + \mathcal{D}$. Rearranging gives $v - x \in \mathcal{D}$, which means $\|v - x\| \leq L$. By the triangle inequality, $\|x\| < R$, i.e. $x \in \mathcal{B}_d(L)$, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound: ball covered by fundamental-domain translates

nodes.name: Upper bound: translates lie in a larger ball
nodes.statement: For the second inequality, we prove that $\bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R)} (x + \mathcal{D}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}_d(R + L)$. Consider a vector $x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R)$ and a vector $y \in x + \mathcal{D}$. From above, we know $\|x\| < R$ and $\|y - x\| \leq L$, so $\|y\| < R + L$, concluding the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound: translates lie in a larger ball

nodes.name: Lower bound: translates of $\mathcal{D}$ in the ball, count points of $X$
nodes.statement: For the first inequality, we notice that $\bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)} (x + \mathcal{D}) \subseteq \mathcal{B}_d(R)$, because for $x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)$ and $y \in x + \mathcal{D}$, we have $\|x\| < R - L$ and $\|y - x\| \leq L$, so $\|y\| < R$ by triangle inequality. Intersecting both sides with $X$ and simplifying, we have \[ \left(\bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)} (x + \mathcal{D})\right) \cap X = \bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)} ((x + \mathcal{D}) \cap X) \subseteq \mathcal{B}_d(R) \cap X \] Consider the (finite) cardinality on both sides and noting that $|(x + \mathcal{D}) \cap X| = |X / \Lambda|$ for all $x$, we see that $|\Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R - L)||X / \Lambda| \leq |X \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R)|$, as desired.
nodes.statement_short: Lower bound: translates of $\mathcal{D}$ in the ball, count points of $X$

nodes.name: Upper bound by the tiling property
nodes.statement: The proof of the second inequality is similar. We again observe that $\mathcal{B}_d(R) \subseteq \bigcup_{x \in \Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R + L)} (x + \mathcal{D})$, which follows from the tiling property of fundamental domain (i.e. every point can be translated by a $\Lambda$ lattice point into $\mathcal{D}$). Intersecting both sides with $X$ and considering cardinality of both sides concludes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Upper bound by the tiling property

nodes.name: Lean technicalities
nodes.statement: There are several technicalities when formalising in Lean, such as having to prove $|\Lambda \cap \mathcal{B}_d(R)|$ is countable and finite. Those are handled at \texttt{aux3}.

nodes.name: Combine the three counting lemmas into a sandwich
nodes.statement: Fix any fundamental domain $\mathcal{D}$ (induced by any basis) of the lattice $\Lambda$. Combining \cref{lemma:sp-finite-density-bound}, \cref{lemma:lattice-points-bound} and \cref{lemma:periodic-points-bounds}, we get the following inequality for the \textit{finite} density: \[ |X / \Lambda| \cdot \frac{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(r / 2)}}{\Vol{\R^d / \Lambda}} \cdot \frac{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(R - r / 2 - 2L)}}{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(R)}} \leq \Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(R) \leq |X / \Lambda| \cdot \frac{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(r / 2)}}{\Vol{\R^d / \Lambda}} \cdot \frac{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(R + r / 2 + 2L)}}{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(R)}} \]
nodes.statement_short: Combine the three counting lemmas into a sandwich

nodes.name: Pass to the limit with the ball ratio lemma
nodes.statement: Taking limit on both sides as $R \to \infty$ and apply the Sandwich theorem and \cref{lemma:volume-ball-ratio-limit}, we get \[ \Delta_{\mathcal{P}} = \limsup_{R \to \infty} \Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(R) = \lim_{R \to \infty} \Delta_{\mathcal{P}}(R) = |X / \Lambda| \cdot \frac{\Vol{\mathcal{B}_d(r / 2)}}{\Vol{\R^d / \Lambda}} \]
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the limit with the ball ratio lemma

nodes.name: Double inclusion
nodes.statement: We prove each side contains the other side.

nodes.name: $\Lambda_8\subseteq\mathrm{span}_\Z(\B_8)$
nodes.statement: For a vector $\vec{v} \in \Lambda_8 \subseteq \R^8$, we have $\sum_i \vec{v}_i \equiv 0 \pmod{2}$ and $\vec{v}_i$ being either all integers or all half-integers. After some modulo arithmetic, it can be seen that $\B_8^{-1}\vec{v}$ as integer coordinates (i.e. it is congruent to $0$ modulo $1$). Hence, $\vec{v} \in \mathrm{span}_{\Z}(\B_8)$.

nodes.name: $\mathrm{span}_\Z(\B_8)\subseteq\Lambda_8$
nodes.statement: For the opposite direction, we write the vector as $\vec{v} = \sum_i c_i\B_8^i \in \mathrm{span}_{\Z}(\B_8)$ with $c_i$ being integers and $\B_8^i$ being the $i$-th basis vector. Expanding the definition then gives $\vec{v} = \left(c_1 - \frac{1}{2}c_7, -c_1 + c_2 - \frac{1}{2}c_7, \cdots, -\frac{1}{2}c_7\right)$. Again, after some modulo arithmetic, it can be seen that $\sum_i \vec{v}_i$ is indeed $0$ modulo $2$ and are all either integers and half-integers, concluding the proof.

nodes.name: Linear independence not needed
nodes.statement: (Note: this proof doesn't depend on that $\B_8$ is linearly independent.)

nodes.name: Reduce to invertibility
nodes.statement: It suffices to prove that $\B_8 \in \mathrm{GL}_8(\R)$.

nodes.name: Explicit inverse matrix
nodes.statement: We prove this by explicitly defining the inverse matrix $\B_8^{-1}$ and proving $\B_8 \B_8^{-1} = I_8$, which implies that $\det(\B_8)$ is nonzero. See the Lean code for more details.,

nodes.name: WLOG $0\notin X$
nodes.statement: Without loss of generality, assume that $0 \notin X$: if $0 \in X$, then we can add the $f(0)$ term to the sum over nonzero elements of $X$, which, if the sum over the nonzero elements converges absolutely, will be equal to the sum over all of $X$.
nodes.section: 4.2 On the Summability of Schwartz Functions

nodes.name: Schwartz decay bound
nodes.statement: Now, we know that for all $k \in \N$, there exists some constant $C$ such that $|f(x)| \leq C\norm{x}^{-k}$ for all $x \in \R^d$.
nodes.section: 4.2 On the Summability of Schwartz Functions

nodes.name: Compare with inverse-power sum
nodes.statement: Choosing $k$ to be sufficiently large, we see that \[ \sum_{x \in X} |f(x)| \leq \sum_{x \in X} \frac{C}{\norm{x}^{k}} = C \sum_{x \in X} \frac{1}{\norm{x}^k} < \infty. \]
nodes.section: 4.2 On the Summability of Schwartz Functions

nodes.name: Attribution to Cohn-Elkies
nodes.statement: Here we reproduce the proof given in \cite{ElkiesCohn}.

nodes.name: Upper bound by $\sharp(X/\Lambda) f(0)$
nodes.statement: The inequality \begin{equation} \sharp (X/\Lambda)\cdot f(0)\geq \sum_{x\in X}\sum_{y\in X/\Lambda}f(x-y)=\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{y\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{\ell\in \Lambda}f(x-y+l)\end{equation} follows from the condition \eqref{eqn:Cohn-Elkies-condition-1} of the theorem and the assumption on the distances between points in $X$.

nodes.name: Apply Poisson summation
nodes.statement: The equality $$\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{y\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{\ell\in \Lambda}f(x-y+l)=\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{y\in X/\Lambda}\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\,\sum_{m\in \Lambda^*} \widehat{f}(m)\,e^{2\pi i m(x-y)}.$$ follows from the Poisson summation formula.

nodes.name: Rewrite as sum of $\widehat f(m)|\cdot|^2$
nodes.statement: The right hand side of the above equation can be written as $$\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}\sum_{y\in X/\Lambda}\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\,\sum_{m\in \Lambda^*} \widehat{f}(m)\,e^{2\pi i m(x-y)}=\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\,\sum_{m\in \Lambda^*} \widehat{f}(m)\cdot\big|\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}e^{2\pi i m x}\big|^2.$$

nodes.name: Nonnegativity and the $m=0$ term
nodes.statement: Note that $\big|\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}e^{2\pi i m x}\big|^2\geq0$ for all $m\in\Lambda^*$. Moreover, the term corresponding to $m=0$ satisfies $\big|\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}e^{2\pi i 0 x}\big|^2=\sharp (X/\Lambda)^2$.

nodes.name: Lower bound by the $m=0$ term
nodes.statement: Now we use the condition \eqref{eqn:Cohn-Elkies-condition-2} and estimate \begin{equation}\frac{1}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\,\sum_{m\in \Lambda^*} \widehat{f}(m)\cdot\big|\sum_{x\in X/\Lambda}e^{2\pi i m(x-y)}\big|^2 \geq \frac{\sharp (X/\Lambda)^2}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\cdot \widehat{f}(0). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Compare the two bounds
nodes.statement: Comparing inequalities \eqref{eqn: sharp X 1} and \eqref{eqn: sharp X 2} we arrive at $$\frac{\sharp (X/\Lambda)}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\leq \frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}.$$

nodes.name: Translate into the density bound
nodes.statement: Now we see that the density of the periodic packing $\mathcal{P}_X$ with balls of radius $1/2$ is bounded by $$\Delta(\mathcal{P}_X)=\frac{\sharp (X/\Lambda)}{\mathrm{vol}(\mathbb{R}^d/\Lambda)}\cdot{\mathrm{vol}(B_d(0,1/2))}\leq \frac{f(0)}{\widehat{f}(0)}\cdot \mathrm{vol}(B_d(0,1/2)).$$ This finishes the proof of the theorem for periodic packings.

nodes.name: $\dim M_k=1+\dim S_k$
nodes.statement: First we note that for $2 < k$ we have $\dim(M_k(\Gamma_1)) = 1 + \dim S_k(\Gamma_1)$. This follows since we know the $E_k$ are in $M_k$ so by scaling appropriately, any non-cuspform $f \in M_k$ we would have $f - a E_k \in S_k$ for some $a$.

nodes.name: $S_k\cong M_{k-12}$ via division by $\Delta$
nodes.statement: Next, note that $S_k(\Gamma_1)$ is isomorphic to $M_{k-12}(\Gamma_1)$, since if $f \in S_k$ then $f/ \Delta$ is now a modular form (using the product expansion of $\Delta$ and its non-vanishing on $\mathfrak{H}$) of weight $k-12$. Note its important that $f$ is a cuspform so that the quotient by $\Delta$ is a modular form.

nodes.name: Small weights case analysis
nodes.statement: So we only need to know the dimensions of $M_k(\Gamma_1)$ for $0 \le k \le 12$. For $k = 0$ we have $\dim M_0(\Gamma_1) = 1$ by \Cref{thm:nonpos_wt}. For $k = 4$ we have $\dim M_4(\Gamma_1) = 1$ since if there was a cuspform $f$ of weight $4$ then $f/ \Delta$ would be a modular form of negative weight, i.e. zero, so $f=0$. Similarly for $k=6,8,10$. For $k=12$ we have $\dim S_{12}(\Gamma_1) = 1$ since the discriminant form is a cusp form of weight $12$ and any other cusp form of weight $12$ would be a scalar multiple of $\Delta$ (since their ratio would be a modular form of weight $0$). So we have $\dim M_{12}(\Gamma_1) = 2$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $0\le k\le 12$
nodes.statement: So we only need to know the dimensions of $M_k(\Gamma_1)$ for $0 \le k \le 12$.

nodes.name: Weight 0
nodes.statement: For $k = 0$ we have $\dim M_0(\Gamma_1) = 1$ by \Cref{thm:nonpos_wt}.

nodes.name: Weights 4,6,8,10
nodes.statement: For $k = 4$ we have $\dim M_4(\Gamma_1) = 1$ since if there was a cuspform $f$ of weight $4$ then $f/ \Delta$ would be a modular form of negative weight, i.e. zero, so $f=0$. Similarly for $k=6,8,10$.

nodes.name: Weight 12
nodes.statement: For $k=12$ we have $\dim S_{12}(\Gamma_1) = 1$ since the discriminant form is a cusp form of weight $12$ and any other cusp form of weight $12$ would be a scalar multiple of $\Delta$ (since their ratio would be a modular form of weight $0$). So we have $\dim M_{12}(\Gamma_1) = 2$.

nodes.name: Weight 2 is zero by contradiction
nodes.statement: Finally we need to check that $\dim M_2(\Gamma_1) = 0$. Firstly, there can't be any cuspforms here by the same argument as above. So we need to check that there are no modular forms of weight $2$. If we did have one, call it $f$ then $f^2$ would be a non-cuspform of weight $4$ and so $f^2 = a E_4$, where in fact $a=a_0(f)^2$ (since $(f^2-a_0(f)E_4)$ is now a cuspform of weight $4$ which means its zero). Similarly, $f^3 = a_0(f)^3 E_6$. But now taking powers to make them weight $12$ forms we see that $a_0(f)^6(E_4^3 - E_6^2) = 0 = 1728 a_0(f)^6 \Delta$ but $a_0(f) \ne 0$ (since its assumed to not be a cuspform), this would mean $\Delta =0$ which we know can't happen.

nodes.name: Level one vanishing-order bound $r_k$
nodes.statement: We know that $\dim(M_k(\Gamma_1))$ is finite dimensional from the above, now this means that there is some $r_k$ such that any element of $M_k(\Gamma_1)$ vanishing at infinity to degree $> r_k$ must be zero.

nodes.name: Form the product $F$ over coset representatives
nodes.statement: Now take $f \in M_k(\Gamma)$ and vanishes to degree $n$ at infinity, then consider $F = \prod_\gamma f\mid_k \gamma$ where the product is over a set of representatives of $\Gamma_1 \backslash \Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Form the product $F$ over coset representatives

nodes.name: $F$ is level one of weight $kd$
nodes.statement: Then $F$ is a modular form of weight $k d$ where $d = [\Gamma_1: \Gamma]$ and vanishes at infinity to degree at least $n$.

nodes.name: Conclude $f=0$
nodes.statement: So if $n > r_{kd}$ then $F=0$ meaning the $f=0$.

nodes.name: T-transformations from the series
nodes.statement: The last three identities easily follow from the definition. For example, \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-T} follows from \begin{align} \Theta_{2}(z + 1) &= \sum_{n\in\Z}e^{\pi i (n+\frac12)^2 (z + 1)} = \sum_{n \in \Z} e^{\pi i (n + \frac{1}{2})^{2}} e^{\pi i (n + \frac{1}{2})^{2} z} \\ &= \sum_{n \in \Z} e^{\pi i (n^2 + n + \frac{1}{4})} e^{\pi i (n + \frac{1}{2})^{2} z} = \sum_{n \in \Z} (-1)^{n^2 + n}e^{\pi i / 4} e^{\pi i (n + \frac{1}{2})^{2} z} \\ &= e^{\pi i / 4} \Theta_{2}(z) \end{align} and taking 4th power.

nodes.name: Reduce S-identities to two
nodes.statement: \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-S} and \eqref{eqn:H4-transform-S} are equivalent under $z \leftrightarrow -1/z$, so it is enough to show \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-S} and \eqref{eqn:H3-transform-S}.

nodes.name: Introduce the Jacobi theta function
nodes.statement: These identities follow from the identities of the \emph{two-variable} Jacobi theta function, which is defined as (be careful for the variables, where we use $\tau$ instead of $z$) \begin{equation} \theta(z, \tau) = \sum_{n \in \mathbb{Z}} e^{2 \pi i n z + \pi i n^2 \tau} \end{equation} and already formalized by David Loeffler.

nodes.name: Specializations to $\Theta_i$
nodes.statement: This function specialize to the theta functions as \begin{align} \Theta_{2}(\tau) &= e^{\pi i \tau / 4} \theta(-\tau / 2, \tau) \\ \Theta_{3}(\tau) &= \theta(0, \tau) \\ \Theta_{4}(\tau) &= \theta(1/2, \tau) \\ \end{align}

nodes.name: Jacobi theta transformation
nodes.statement: Poisson summation formula gives \begin{equation} \theta(z, \tau) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-i \tau}} e^{-\frac{\pi i z^2}{\tau}} \theta\left(\frac{z}{\tau}, -\frac{1}{\tau}\right) \end{equation} and applying the specializations above yield the identities.

nodes.name: Derive the $S$-identities
nodes.statement: For example, \eqref{eqn:H4-transform-S} follows from \begin{equation} \Theta_{4}(\tau) = \theta\left(\frac{1}{2}, \tau\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-i\tau}} e^{- \frac{\pi i }{4 \tau}} \theta\left(\frac{1}{2 \tau}, -\frac{1}{\tau}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{-i\tau}} \Theta_{2}\left(-\frac{1}{\tau}\right) \end{equation} and taking 4th power.

nodes.name: Reduce to generators $\alpha,\beta,-I$
nodes.statement: By \cref{lemma:Gamma-2-generators} and \cref{lemma:slash-operator-chain-rule}, it suffices to show that the $H_i$ are invariant under slash actions with respect to $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $-I$.

nodes.name: $-I$ acts trivially
nodes.statement: Invariance under $-I$ follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:slash-negI-even-weight}.

nodes.name: Use transformation rules and matrix identities
nodes.statement: The rest follows from Lemma \ref{lemma:slash-operator-chain-rule}, \ref{lemma:theta-transform-S-T}, and the matrix identities \begin{equation} \alpha = T^2, \quad \beta = -S\alpha^{-1}S = -ST^{-2}S. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Use transformation rules and matrix identities

nodes.name: Compute for $H_2$
nodes.statement: For example, invariance for $H_2$ can be proved by \begin{align} H_2|\alpha &= H_2 |T^{2} = -H_2 |T = H_2 \\ H_2|\beta &= H_2 |(-S\alpha^{-1}S) = H_2 | (S\alpha^{-1}S) =-H_4 |(\alpha^{-1}S) = -H_4 |S = H_2. \end{align}

nodes.name: Goal: boundedness at $i\infty$
nodes.statement: We want to show that for $\gamma \in \Gamma_1$, $\|H_2|_2\gamma(z)\|$ is bounded as $z \in \mathbb{H} \to i\infty$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $H_2,H_3,H_4$
nodes.statement: Firstly, by \Cref{lemma:theta-transform-S-T}, \Cref{lemma:Gamma-2-generators} and induction on group elements, we notice that $\{\pm H_2, \pm H_3, \pm H_4\}$ is closed under action by $\Gamma_1$. Hence, it suffices to prove that $H_2$, $H_3$ and $H_4$ are bounded at $i\infty$.

nodes.name: Termwise bound of the theta series
nodes.statement: Consider $z \in \mathbb{H}$ with $\Im(z) \geq A$. We proceed by direct algebraic manipulation: \begin{align} \|H_2(z)\| &= \left\|\sum_{n \in \Z} \exp\left(\pi i \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 z\right)\right\|^4 \leq \left(\sum_{n \in \Z} \left\|\exp\left(\pi i \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 z\right)\right)\right\|^4 \\ &= \left(\sum_{n \in \Z} \left\|\exp\left(-\pi \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 \Im(z)\right)\right)\right\|^4 \leq \left(\sum_{n \in \Z} \left\|\exp\left(-\pi \left(n + \frac{1}{2}\right)^2 A\right)\right)\right\|^4 \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Termwise bound of the theta series

nodes.name: Convergence via Jacobi theta
nodes.statement: Where we prove the final term is convergent by noticing that it equals $\exp(-\pi A / 4)\theta(iA / 2, iA)$, which has been shown to converge in \texttt{Mathlib}. The proofs for $H_3$ and $H_4$ are similar (actually easier) and have been omitted. \todo{It seems the \texttt{MDifferentiable} requirement is missing.}

nodes.name: Define $f$, a weight 4 form for $\Gamma(2)$
nodes.statement: Let $f = (H_2 + H_4 - H_3)^{2}$. Obviously, $f$ is a modular form of weight $4$ and level $\Gamma(2)$.

nodes.name: $f$ is $S$- and $T$-invariant
nodes.statement: However, by using the transformation rules of $H_2, H_3, H_4$, one have \begin{align} f|_{S} &= (-H_4 - H_2 + H_3)^{2} = f\\ f|_{T} &= (-H_2 + H_3 - H_4)^{2} = f \end{align} so $f$ is actually a modular form of level $1$.

nodes.name: $f$ is a level one cusp form of weight 4, so zero
nodes.statement: By considering the limit as $z \to i\infty$, $f$ is a cusp form, so we get $f = 0$ from \eqref{eqn:dimS4}.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is a level one cusp form of weight 4, so zero

nodes.name: Same method as the Jacobi identity
nodes.statement: We can prove these similarly as Lemma \ref{lemma:jacobi-identity}.
nodes.statement_short: Same method as the Jacobi identity

nodes.name: RHS are level one forms
nodes.statement: Right hand sides of \eqref{eqn:e4theta}, \eqref{eqn:e6theta}, and \eqref{eqn:disctheta} are all modular forms of level $\Gamma_1$ and desired weights, where \eqref{eqn:disctheta} is a cusp form since $H_2$ is.

nodes.name: Dimension one and leading coefficients
nodes.statement: Now the identities follow from the dimension calculations $\dim M_4(\Gamma_1) = \dim M_6(\Gamma_1) = \dim S_{12}(\Gamma_1) = 1$ and comparing the first nonzero $q$-coefficients.

nodes.name: Write out the slash action
nodes.statement: Let $G = \partial_{k}F = F' - \frac{k}{12}E_2 F$. From $F \in M_k(\Gamma)$, we have \begin{equation} (F|_{k}\gamma)(z) := (cz + d)^{-k} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right), \quad \gamma = \begin{pmatrix}a & b \\ c & d\end{pmatrix} \in \Gamma. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Differentiate the slash action
nodes.statement: By taking the derivative of the above equation, we get \begin{align} \frac{\dd}{\dd z}(F|_{k} \gamma)(z) &= -kc (cz + d)^{-k - 1} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) + (cz + d)^{-k} (cz + d)^{-2} \frac{\dd F}{\dd z}\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) \\ &= -kc (cz + d)^{-k - 1} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) + (cz + d)^{-k - 2} \frac{\dd F}{\dd z}\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) \\ &= -kc (cz + d)^{-k - 1} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) + 2 \pi i (cz + d)^{-k - 2} F'\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) \\ \Leftrightarrow (F|_{k} \gamma)'(z) &= -\frac{kc}{2 \pi i} (cz + d)^{-k - 1} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) + (cz + d)^{-k - 2} F'\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right). \end{align}

nodes.name: Combine with $E_2$ law
nodes.statement: Combined with \eqref{eqn:E2-transform-general}, we get \begin{align} ((\partial_k F)|_{k+2}\gamma)(z) &= (cz + d)^{-k-2} \left(F'\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) - \frac{k}{12}E_2\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right)F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right)\right) \\ &= (cz + d)^{-k-2} F'\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) - \frac{k}{12} \left(E_2(z) - \frac{6ic}{\pi(cz + d)}\right) \cdot (cz + d)^{-k} F\left(\frac{az + b}{cz + d}\right) \\ &= (F|_{k}\gamma)'(z) - \frac{k}{12} E_2(z) (F|_{k}\gamma)(z) \\ &= \partial_{k} (F|_{k}\gamma)(z). \end{align}

nodes.name: Reformulate via Serre derivatives
nodes.statement: In terms of Serre derivatives, these are equivalent to \begin{align} \partial_{1}E_2 &= -\frac{1}{12} E_4 \\ \partial_{4}E_4 &= -\frac{1}{3} E_6 \\ \partial_{6}E_6 &= -\frac{1}{2} E_4^2 \end{align}

nodes.name: Serre derivatives are modular
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:serre-der-modularity}, all the Serre derivatives are, in fact, modular. To be precise, the modularity of $\partial_{4} E_4$ and $\partial_6 E_6$ directly follows from Theorem \ref{thm:serre-der-modularity}, and that of $\partial_{1}E_2$ follows from \eqref{eqn:E2-transform-general}.

nodes.name: Transformation of $E_2'$ and $E_2^2$
nodes.statement: Differentiating and squaring then gives us the following: \begin{align} E_2'|_{4}\gamma &= E_2' - \frac{ic}{\pi(cz + d)} E_2 - \frac{3c^2}{\pi^2 (cz + d)^2} \\ E_2^2|_{4}\gamma &= E_2^2 - \frac{12ic}{\pi(cz + d)} E_2 - \frac{36c^2}{\pi^2 (cz + d)^2} \end{align} Hence, \eqref{eqn:DE2}$-\frac{1}{12}$\eqref{eqn:E2sq-transform} is a modular form of weight 4.

nodes.name: Determine constants by dimensions
nodes.statement: By \Cref{cor:dim-mf}, they should be multiples of $E_4, E_6, E_4^2$, and the proportionality constants can be determined by observing the constant terms of $q$-expansions.

nodes.name: Define defects $f_2,f_3,f_4$
nodes.statement: Equivalences are obvious from the definition of the Serre derivative. Define $f_{2}, f_{3}, f_{4}$ be the differences of the left and right hand sides of \eqref{eqn:H2-serre-der}, \eqref{eqn:H3-serre-der}, \eqref{eqn:H4-serre-der}. \begin{align} f_{2} &:= \partial_{2} H_{2} - \frac{1}{6} H_{2}(H_{2} + 2H_{4}) \\ f_{3} &:= \partial_{2} H_{3} - \frac{1}{6} (H_{2}^2 - H_{4}^2) \\ f_{4} &:= \partial_{2} H_{4} + \frac{1}{6} H_{4}(2H_{2} + H_{4}). \end{align}

nodes.name: Goal: show they vanish
nodes.statement: Then these are a priori modular forms of weight $4$ and level $\Gamma(2)$, and our goal is to prove that they are actually zeros.

nodes.name: $f_2+f_4=f_3$
nodes.statement: By Jacobi's identity \eqref{eqn:jacobi-identity}, we have $f_{2} + f_{4} = f_{3}$.

nodes.name: Transformations of $f_2,f_4$
nodes.statement: Also, the transformation rules of $H_2, H_3, H_4$ give \begin{align} f_{2}|_{S} &= -f_{4} \\ f_{2}|_{T} &= -f_{2} \\ f_{4}|_{S} &= -f_{2} \\ f_{4}|_{T} &= f_{3} = f_{2} + f_{4}. \end{align}

nodes.name: $g,h$ are level one
nodes.statement: Then one can check that both $g$ and $h$ are invariant under the actions of $S$ and $T$, hence they are modular forms of level $1$.

nodes.name: $g=h=0$ by dimension
nodes.statement: Also, by analyzing the limit of $g$ and $h$ as $z \to i \infty$, one can see that $g$ and $h$ are cusp forms, hence $g = h = 0$ by \eqref{eqn:dimS6} and \eqref{eqn:dimS8}.

nodes.name: Deduce $f_2=0$
nodes.statement: This implies \begin{align} 3 E_4 f_2^{2} &= 3 (H_2^2 + H_2 H_4 + H_4^2) f_2^{2} = ((2 H_2 + H_4)^{2} - (2H_2 + H_4)(H_2 + 2H_4) + (H_2 + 2H_4)^{2}) f_2^{2}\\ &= (2 H_2 + H_4)^{2} (f_2^2 + f_2 f_4 + f_4^2) = 0 \end{align} and by considering $q$-series ($E_4$ has an invertible $q$-series), we get $f_2 = 0$.

nodes.name: Bound the quotient
nodes.statement: By the product formula \eqref{eqn:disc-definition}, \begin{align} \left|\frac{f(z)}{\Delta(z)}\right| &= \left|\frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} c_f(n) e^{\pi i n z}}{e^{2 \pi i z}\prod_{n \ge 1} (1 - e^{2\pi i n z})^{24}}\right| \\ &= |e^{\pi i (n_0 - 2)z}| \cdot \frac{|\sum_{n \ge n_0} c_f(n) e^{\pi i (n - n_0) z}|}{\prod_{n \ge 1} |1 - e^{2\pi i n z}|^{24}} \\ &\le e^{-\pi (n_0 - 2) \Im z} \cdot \frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} |c_f(n)| e^{-\pi (n - n_0) \Im z}}{\prod_{n \ge 1} (1 - e^{- 2\pi n \Im z})^{24}} \\ &\le e^{-\pi (n_0 - 2) \Im z} \cdot \frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} |c_f(n)| e^{-\pi (n - n_0) / 2}}{\prod_{n \ge 1} (1 - e^{-\pi n})^{24}} \\ &= C_f \cdot e^{-\pi (n_0 - 2) \Im z} \end{align} where \begin{equation} C_f = \frac{\sum_{n \ge n_0} |c_f(n)| e^{-\pi (n - n_0) / 2}}{\prod_{n \ge 1} (1 - e^{-\pi n})^{24}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Convergence of the constant
nodes.statement: Note that the summation in the numerator converges absolutely because of polynomial growth. The denominator also converges, which is simply $e^{\pi} \cdot \Delta(i/2)$.

nodes.name: Bound $r^n e^{-\pi r/s}\le Cs^n$
nodes.statement: Fix $n \in \N$. We know there exists a constant $C$ such that for all $x \geq 0$, $\abs{x}^n \cdot \abs{e^{-\pi x}} \leq C$. In particular, for all $r \geq 0$ and $s \geq 1$, $r^n \cdot e^{-\pi r/s} \leq C s^n$.

nodes.name: Bound the integral
nodes.statement: Hence, for all $r \in \R$, we can write \begin{align} r^n \cdot \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, e^{-\pi r /s} \, \dd{s} = \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, \left(\abs{r}^n \cdot e^{-\pi r /s}\right) \, \dd{s} \leq C \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} \end{align}
nodes.section: 7 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points

nodes.name: Recall Gamma function
nodes.statement: The $\Gamma$ function is given by \begin{align} \Gamma(x) = \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-u} \, u^{x-1} \, \dd{u} \end{align} for all $x > 0$.
nodes.section: 7 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points

nodes.name: Evaluate via $\Gamma(n+1)=n!$
nodes.statement: Hence, writing $u = 2\pi s$ and using $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$, we get \begin{align} C \int_{1}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} \leq C \int_{0}^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, s^n \, \dd{s} = C \int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n+1}} e^{-u} \, u^n \, \dd{u} = \frac{C}{(2\pi)^n} \Gamma(n+1) = \frac{C \cdot n!}{(2\pi)^n} \end{align} Defining $C' := \frac{C \cdot n!}{(2\pi)^n}$ finishes the proof.

nodes.name: Reduce to $I_1$
nodes.statement: We only prove the bound for $I_1(r)$, as the other two are similar.

nodes.name: Substitute $z=-1+it$
nodes.statement: By the change of variable $z = -1 + i t$ for $t \in [0,1]$, we have $$ I_1(r) = -i \int_0^1 \phi_0\left(\frac{-1}{i t}\right) t^2 e^{-\pi i r} \cdot e^{-\pi r t} \, \dd t. $$

nodes.name: Substitute $s=1/t$ and bound
nodes.statement: With the change of variable $s = 1 / t$, we get $$ I_1(r) = i \int_1^{\infty} \phi_0(i s) \cdot s^{-4} \cdot e^{-\pi i r} \cdot e^{-\pi r / s} \, \dd s $$ and the absolute value can be bounded as $$ |I_1(r)| \leq \int_1^{\infty} |\phi_0(i s)| \cdot s^{-4} \cdot |e^{-\pi i r}| \cdot e^{-\pi r / s} \, \dd s \le \int_1^{\infty} |\phi_0(is)| \cdot e^{-\pi r / s} \, \dd s. $$

nodes.name: Apply $\phi_0$ bound
nodes.statement: Now, Corollary~\ref{cor:phi0-bound} shows $$ |I_1(r)| \leq C_0 \int_1^{\infty} e^{-2\pi s} \, e^{-\pi r / s} \, \dd s. $$

nodes.name: Parametrize $I_2$
nodes.statement: For $I_2(r)$, parametrize $z$ as $z = t + i$ for $t \in [-1,0]$, and we have $$ I_2(r) = \int_{-1}^0 \phi_0\left(\frac{-1}{t + 1 + i}\right) (t + 1 + i)^2 e^{\pi i r t} e^{-\pi r} \, \dd t. $$

nodes.name: Bound $I_2$ (and $I_4$)
nodes.statement: Since the function $z \mapsto \phi_0\left(\frac{-1}{z+1}\right) (z+1)^2$ is holomorphic and bounded on the contour, there exists $C > 0$ such that $|\phi_0\left(\frac{-1}{z+1}\right) (z + 1)^2| \leq C$, and the absolute value of the integral can be bounded by $$ |I_2(r)| \le \int_{-1}^{0} C e^{-\pi r} \, \dd t = C e^{-\pi r}. $$ The bound for $I_4(r)$ is similar.

nodes.name: Parametrize and bound $I_6$
nodes.statement: For $I_6(r)$, parametrize $z$ as $z = i t$ for $t \in [1, \infty)$, and we have $$ I_6(r) = 2 i \int_1^{\infty} \phi_0(i t) e^{-\pi r t} \, \dd t $$ and the absolute value can be bounded as (using Corollary~\ref{cor:phi0-bound}) $$ |I_6(r)| \leq 2 \int_1^{\infty} |\phi_0(i t)| e^{-\pi r t} \, \dd t \leq \frac{2C_0}{\pi} \int_1^{\infty} e^{-2\pi t} e^{-\pi r t} \, \dd t = \frac{2C_0}{\pi} \frac{e^{-\pi (r + 2)}}{r + 2}. $$

nodes.name: Reduce to smoothness and decay
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:smooth-fast-decay-schwartz}, it suffices to show that the function is smooth and decays faster than any polynomial.

nodes.name: Smoothness
nodes.statement: The smoothness follows from the ``differentiation under the integral'', which is already formalized in \texttt{mathlib}.

nodes.name: Decay from the integral bounds
nodes.statement: The decay follows from Lemmas \ref{lem:bound-I1-I3-I5} and \ref{lem:bound-I2-I4-I6}, together with Lemma \ref{lem:integral-bound}.

nodes.name: Recall Gaussian Fourier transform
nodes.statement: We recall that the Fourier transform of a Gaussian function is \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}(e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z})(y)=z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z}) }. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Exchange integrals
nodes.statement: Next, we exchange the contour integration with respect to $z$ variable and Fourier transform with respect to $x$ variable in \eqref{eqn:a-definition}. This can be done, since the corresponding double integral converges absolutely. In this way we obtain \begin{align} \widehat{a}(y)=&\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz +\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz\notag \\ -&2\int\limits_{0}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz +2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,(\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz.\notag \end{align}

nodes.name: Substitute $w=-1/z$
nodes.statement: Now we make a change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$. We obtain \begin{align} \widehat{a}(y)=&\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(1-\frac{1}{w-1}\Big)\,(\frac{-1}{w}+1)^2\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw\notag\\ +&\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(1-\frac{1}{w+1}\Big)\,(\frac{-1}{w}-1)^2\,w^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw\\ -&2\int\limits_{i \infty}^i\phi_0(w)\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw +2\int\limits_{i}^{0}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,w}\,dw.\notag \end{align}

nodes.name: Use periodicity to recover $a$
nodes.statement: Since $\phi_0$ is $1$-periodic we have \begin{align} \widehat{a}(y)\,=\,&\int\limits_{1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz +\int\limits_{-1}^i\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz\notag \\ +&2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|y\|^2 \,z}\,dz\notag \\ \,=\,&a(y). \end{align} This finishes the proof of the proposition.

From \eqref{eqn:phi0-trans-S} we deduce that if $r>\sqrt{2}$ then $\phi_0\Big( rac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}	o 0$ as $\Im(z)	o\infty$. Now from \eqref{eqn:phi0-trans-S} we find  egin{align}&\phi_0\Big( rac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2-2\phi_0\Big( rac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2+ \phi_0\Big( rac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2=

nodes.name: Recover $a(r)$
nodes.statement: Thus, we obtain \begin{align} d(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z+1}\Big)\,(z+1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z}\Big)\,z^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\notag\\ +&\int\limits_{1}^{i}\phi_0\Big(\frac{-1}{z-1}\Big)\,(z-1)^2\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz +2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\phi_0(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=a(r).\notag \end{align} This finishes the proof.

nodes.name: For $r>\sqrt2$ use double-zero formula
nodes.statement: Suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop:a-double-zeros} $$a(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\phi_0(i/t)\,t^2\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$

nodes.name: Exchange integrals
nodes.statement: We use identity~\eqref{eqn:gaussian Fourier} and change contour integration in $z$ and Fourier transform in $x$. Thus we obtain \begin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz + \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz \notag \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,z^{-4}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 (\frac{-1}{z})}\,dz. \notag \end{align}

nodes.name: Substitute $w=-1/z$
nodes.statement: We make the change of variables $w=\frac{-1}{z}$ and arrive at \begin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw \notag \\ -& 2\,\int\limits_{i\infty}^{i}\psi_I\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw - 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{0}\psi_S\Big(\frac{-1}{w}\Big)\,w^{2}\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.\notag \end{align}

nodes.statement:
Now we observe that the definitions \eqref{eqn:psiI-define}--\eqref{eqn:psiS-define} imply  egin{align} \psi_T|_{-2}S=&-\psi_T 
otag \ \psi_I|_{-2}S=&\psi_S

nodes.name: Rewrite integrals
nodes.statement: Therefore, we arrive at \begin{align} \mathcal{F}(b)(x)= & \int\limits_{1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + \int\limits_{-1}^{i}-\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz \notag \\ +& 2\,\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_S(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 z}\,dz + 2\,\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i \|x\|^2 w}\,dw.\notag \end{align}

nodes.name: Name RHS $c(r)$; convergence
nodes.statement: We denote the right hand side of~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} by $c(r)$. By Corollary \ref{cor:psiI-near-0-infty}, the integral in~\eqref{eqn: b double zeroes} converges for $r>\sqrt{2}$.

nodes.name: Split the integral
nodes.statement: Then we rewrite it in the following way: $$c(r)=\int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz-2\int\limits_{0}^{i\infty}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.$$

nodes.name: Deform contours
nodes.statement: From the Fourier expansion~\eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we know that $\psi_I(z)=e^{-2\pi i z}+O(1)$ as $\Im(z)\to\infty$. By assumption $r^2>2$, hence we can deform the path of integration and write \begin{align} \int\limits_{-1}^{i\infty-1}\psi_I(z+1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ \int\limits_{1}^{i\infty+1}\psi_I(z-1)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz=& \int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz. \end{align}

nodes.name: Collect terms
nodes.statement: We have \begin{align}c(r)=&\int\limits_{-1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz+\int\limits_{1}^{i}\psi_T(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz -2\int\limits_{0}^{i}\psi_I(z)\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz\\ &+2\int\limits_{i}^{i\infty}(\psi_T(z)-\psi_I(z))\,e^{\pi i r^2 \,z}\,dz.\nonumber \end{align}

nodes.name: Identity $\psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I$
nodes.statement: Next, we check that the functions $\psi_I,\psi_T$, and $\psi_S$ satisfy the following identity: \begin{equation}\psi_T+\psi_S=\psi_I.\end{equation} Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn:psiI-define}-\eqref{eqn:psiS-define} we get \begin{align}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S\notag\\ =&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.\notag\end{align} Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$ Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore, $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h|_{-2}-h|ST=\psi_I.$$
nodes.section: 7 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points

nodes.name: Expand definitions
nodes.statement: Indeed, from definitions \eqref{eqn:psiI-define}-\eqref{eqn:psiS-define} we get \begin{align}\psi_T+\psi_S=&(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}T+(h-h|_{-2}ST)|_{-2}S\notag\\ =&h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}ST^2+h|_{-2}S-h|_{-2}STS.\notag\end{align}
nodes.section: 7 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points

nodes.name: Use $\Gamma_0(2)$-invariance of $h$
nodes.statement: Note that $ST^2S$ belongs to $\Gamma_0(2)$. Thus, since $h\in M^!_{-2}\Gamma_0(2)$ we get $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS. $$

nodes.name: Conclude the identity
nodes.statement: Now we observe that $T$ and $STS(ST)^{-1}$ are also in $\Gamma_0(2)$. Therefore, $$\psi_T+\psi_S=h|_{-2}T-h|_{-2}STS=h|_{-2}-h|ST=\psi_I.$$
nodes.section: 7 Fourier eigenfunctions with double zeroes at lattice points

nodes.name: Recover $b(r)$
nodes.statement:

nodes.name: For $r>\sqrt2$ use double-zero formula
nodes.statement: First, suppose that $r>\sqrt{2}$. Then by Proposition~\ref{prop:b-double-zeros} $$b(r)=4i\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_{0}^{\infty}\psi_I(it)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt. $$

nodes.name: Asymptotics of $\psi_I(it)$
nodes.statement: From \eqref{eqn: psi fourier I} we obtain \begin{equation} \psi_I(it)=e^{2\pi t}+144+O(e^{-\pi t})\quad\mbox{as}\;t\to\infty. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Integrate principal part
nodes.statement: For $r>\sqrt{2}$ we have \begin{equation} \int\limits_0^\infty \left(e^{2\pi t}+144\right)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt =\frac{1}{\pi\,(r^2-2)}+\frac{144}{\pi\,r^2}.\end{equation}

nodes.statement: On the other hand, from the definition \eqref{eqn:b-definition} we see that $b(r)$ is analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Analyticity of the RHS
nodes.statement: The asymptotic expansion \eqref{eqn: psi asymptotic} implies that the right hand side of \eqref{eqn:b-another-integral} is also analytic in some neighborhood of $[0,\infty)$.

nodes.name: Extend by analytic continuation
nodes.statement: Hence, the identity \eqref{eqn:b-another-integral} holds on the whole interval $[0,\infty)$. This finishes the proof of the proposition.

nodes.name: Express $\psi_I(it)$ via $\psi_S(i/t)$
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eqn:psiS-define}, \begin{equation} \psi_I(it) = (\psi_S|_{-2}S)(it) = (it)^{2}\psi_S\left(-\frac{1}{it}\right) = -t^2 \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Rewrite $A(t)<0$ in $F,G$
nodes.statement: Combined with Lemma \ref{lemma:F-G-phi-psi-identities} we can rewrite \eqref{eqn:ineqA} as \begin{equation} A(t) = -t^2 \phi_0\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) + \frac{36}{\pi^2} \psi_S\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) < 0 \Leftrightarrow \frac{F(it)}{\Delta(it)} + \frac{18}{\pi^2} \frac{G(it)}{\Delta(it)} > 0 \end{equation} for $t > 0$, which is equivalent to \eqref{eqn:ineqAnew} by Corollary \ref{cor:disc-pos}.

nodes.name: Same for $B$
nodes.statement: Equivalences of \eqref{eqn:ineqB} and \eqref{eqn:ineqBnew} follows similarly; just change the sign.

nodes.name: Direct computation
nodes.statement: Both can be shown by direct computations.

nodes.name: Same for $G$
nodes.statement: Similarly, \eqref{eqn:ddg} can be proved using Proposition \ref{prop:theta-der} and Lemma \ref{lemma:lv1-lv2-identities}.

nodes.name: Substitute $t\to1/t$
nodes.statement: We have \begin{equation} \lim_{t \to 0^+} Q(t) = \lim_{t \to 0^+} \frac{F(it)}{G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F(i/t)}{G(i/t)}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Transform $F,G$
nodes.statement: By using the transformation laws of Eisenstein series \eqref{eqn:E2-S-transform}, \eqref{eqn:Ek-trans-S} (for $k = 4, 6$) and the thetanull functions, \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-S}, \eqref{eqn:H4-transform-S}, we get \begin{align} F\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) &= t^{12} F(it) - \frac{12t^{11}}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36t^{10}}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2, \\ G\left(\frac{i}{t}\right) &= t^{10} H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2}). \end{align}

nodes.name: Cusp forms decay
nodes.statement: Since $F$, $E_2 E_4 - E_6$ and $H_2$ are cusp forms, we have $\lim_{t \to \infty}t^k A(it) = 0$ when $A(z)$ is one of these forms and $k \geq 0$.

nodes.name: Evaluate the limit
nodes.statement: From $\lim_{t \to \infty} E_4(it) = 1 = \lim_{t \to \infty}H_{4}(it)$, we get \begin{align} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{F(i/t)}{G(i/t)} &= \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{t^{12} F(it) - \frac{12t^{11}}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36t^{10}}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2}{t^{10} H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2})} \\ &= \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{t^{2} F(it) - \frac{12t}{\pi} (E_2(it)E_4(it) - E_6(it))E_4(it) + \frac{36}{\pi^2}E_4(it)^2}{H_{4}(it)^{3}(2H_{4}(it)^{2} + 5 H_{4}(it)H_{2}(it) + 5 H_{2}(it)^{2})} \\ &= \frac{18}{\pi^2}. \end{align}

nodes.name: Reduce to positivity of $\mathcal{L}_{1,0}$
nodes.statement: It is enough to show that \begin{align} \frac{\dd}{\dd t} \left(\frac{F(it)}{G(it)}\right) < 0 &\Leftrightarrow (- 2\pi) \frac{F'(it)G(it) - F(it) G'(it)}{G(it)^{2}} < 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow F'(it) G(it) - F(it) G'(it) > 0 \\ &\Leftrightarrow (\partial_{10}F)(it) G(it) - F(it) (\partial_{10}G)(it) > 0. \end{align}

nodes.name: Define $\mathcal{L}_{1,0}$
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0} := (\partial_{10}F) G - F (\partial_{10} G) = F'G - FG'$. Then \begin{align} \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}}{FG} = \frac{F'G - FG'}{FG} = \frac{F'}{F} - \frac{G'}{G} \end{align}

nodes.name: Positive near infinity
nodes.statement: The vanishing order of $F$ and $G$ at the infinity are $2$ and $\frac{3}{2}$ respectively, so by Lemma \ref{lemma:log-der-inf}, we have \begin{align} \lim_{t \to \infty} \frac{\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it)}{F(it) G(it)} = \lim_{t \to \infty} \left(\frac{F'(it)}{F(it)} - \frac{G'(it)}{G(it)}\right) = 2 - \frac{3}{2} = \frac{1}{2} > 0 \end{align} so $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it) > 0$ for sufficiently large $t$.

nodes.name: Serre derivative positive
nodes.statement: Its Serre derivative $\partial_{22} \mathcal{L}_{1, 0}$ is positive by Corollary \ref{cor:MLDE-pos}: \begin{align} \partial_{22} \mathcal{L}_{1, 0} = (\partial_{12} \partial_{10} F) G - F (\partial_{12}\partial_{10} G) = \Delta (7200 (-E_{2}') G + 640 H_2 F) > 0. \end{align}

nodes.name: Apply positivity criterion
nodes.statement: Hence $\mathcal{L}_{1, 0}(it) > 0$ by Theorem \ref{thm:anti-serre-der-pos}, and the monotonicity follows.

nodes.name: Prove condition (g1)
nodes.statement: First, we prove that \eqref{eqn:g1} holds. By Propositions~\ref{prop:a-double-zeros} and \ref{prop:b-double-zeros} we know that for $r>\sqrt{2}$ \begin{equation} g(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty A(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$A(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ from the Proposition~\ref{prop:ineqA} we know that $A(t)<0\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,\infty).$ Therefore identity \eqref{eqn:g A} implies \eqref{eqn:g1}.

nodes.name: Express $g$ via $A$; $A<0$
nodes.statement: By Propositions~\ref{prop:a-double-zeros} and \ref{prop:b-double-zeros} we know that for $r>\sqrt{2}$ \begin{equation} g(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty A(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$A(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)-\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$ from the Proposition~\ref{prop:ineqA} we know that $A(t)<0\quad\mbox{for}\;t\in(0,\infty).$

nodes.name: Conclude (g1)
nodes.statement: Therefore identity \eqref{eqn:g A} implies \eqref{eqn:g1}.

nodes.name: Express $\widehat g$ via $B$
nodes.statement: Next, we prove \eqref{eqn:g2}. By Propositions~\ref{prop:a-another-integral} and~\ref{prop:b-another-integral} we know that for $r>0$ \begin{equation} \widehat{g}(r)=\frac{\pi}{2160}\,\sin(\pi r^2/2)^2\,\int\limits_0^\infty B(t)\,e^{-\pi r^2 t}\,dt\end{equation} where $$B(t)=-t^2\phi_0(i/t)+\frac{36}{\pi^2}\,\psi_I(it).$$

nodes.name: Values at 0 give (g3)
nodes.statement: Finally, the property \eqref{eqn:g3} readily follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:a0} and Proposition~\ref{prop:b0}. This finishes the proof of Theorems~\ref{thm:g1} and~\ref{thm:g}.

nodes.name: Invariance under generators of $\Gamma_0(2)$
nodes.statement: Indeed, first we check that $h|_{-2}\gamma=h$ for all $\gamma\in\Gamma_0(2)$. Since the group $\Gamma_0(2)$ is generated by elements $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\2&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ it suffices to check that $h$ is invariant under their action. This follows immediately from \eqref{eqn:H2-transform-S}--\eqref{eqn:H4-transform-S} and \eqref{eqn: h define}.

nodes.statement: Next we analyze the poles of $h$. It is known \cite[Chapter~I Lemma~4.1]{Mumford} that $\theta_{10}$ has no zeros in the upper-half plane and hence $h$ has poles only at the cusps.
